candidateRows: Important notions of freedom and willing can survive determinism without alternative possibilities or ultimate sourcehood.
This states the compatibilist side's governing thesis and reframes the debate around practically important forms of freedom and willing that remain available under determinism.

After defining libertarianism and incompatibilist determinism, Joe presents compatibilism as identifying valuable forms of freedom and will rather than preserving the libertarian conception unchanged.
Libertarian freedom best captures deliberative experience, and there is no adequate reason to reject that experience as unreal.
This supplies the libertarian side's foundational positive case from experienced control, genuine options, selection, and agency while distinguishing causal from non-causal determination.

Nathan describes ordinary deliberation as considering genuine alternatives and selecting among them, argues that this phenomenology supports libertarianism, and specifies the kind of determinism he rejects.
Determinative relations need not be causal, because logical and mathematical entailment lacks the pushing, forcing, and temporal features of causation.
The distinction is structurally important because later arguments on both sides turn on whether determination itself implies causal constraint or external control over an agent.
Using mathematical squaring as an example, Nathan explains that one fact can necessitate another without causing it and contrasts entailment with temporally sequenced force or restraint.
Scientific presentations of free-will denial often assume interpretive commitments rather than proving them, so the issue remains complex and unsettled.
This challenges a major motivation for denying libertarian freedom by arguing that scientific evidence does not independently settle the philosophical questions about causation, time, and agency.
Popular scientific arguments claiming that empirical research has already established that human beings lack free will.

Nathan contrasts the complexity of specialist work on free will, causation, and time with simplified popular treatments, warning that methodological assumptions are often presented as scientific conclusions.
Directed deliberation and differentiated brain systems undermine the claim that choices merely appear unbidden or are settled before conscious agency.
This directly defends deliberative agency against both an introspective objection and the claim that neuroscience shows conscious choice to be merely retrospective or causally idle.
Sam Harris's claims that thoughts simply arise without deliberative choice and that brain activity predicts decisions before conscious awareness.

Nathan describes deliberation as a directed process involving imagination, rational and emotional evaluation, then appeals to differentiated neural control systems as consistent with that subjective process.
Current neuroscience is too young and indirect to bear decisive philosophical weight against free will.
This blocks an empirical route to hard incompatibilism while preserving the compatibilist's ability to discuss agency without depending on disputed interpretations of immature measurement techniques.
The preceding discussion that treats Libet-style experiments and neural measurements as evidence capable of resolving whether people possess free will.
Joe emphasizes that tools such as fMRI measure proxies like blood flow, notes the field's youth, and lowers confidence in experiments that specialists have methodologically questioned.
On a monist or physicalist view, a brain state is part of the person, so neural causation does not displace personal agency.

This rebuts the inference from prior neural activity to absence of agency by denying the supposed competition between a person and that person's brain, thereby preserving freedom under physical determination.
The objection that an action predicted or initiated by a prior brain state was performed by the brain rather than by the person.
Joe separates causal from non-causal determination and argues that treating the brain as a rival cause to the person imports a dualistic separation inconsistent with monism or physicalism.
Even in a deterministic world, meaningful distinctions between willing and unwilling action, including consent, survive and support compatibilist agency.

The move identifies a concrete, morally and practically important kind of freedom that survives determinism and explains why non-causal determination need not reduce agents to externally controlled puppets.

Joe asks what distinctions remain useful under determinism, highlights consent and the difference between willed and unwilled decisions, and argues that the puppeteer image depends specifically on causal determinism.
Libet-style readiness-potential findings do not show that unconscious brain activity causes conscious decisions or subsequent actions.
This is a detailed causal rebuttal to a prominent neuroscientific challenge, arguing through dissociations that readiness potential can occur without either conscious choice or motor action.
The claim that predictive neural activity and Libet readiness potentials establish that unconscious brain processes cause decisions before conscious willing occurs.

Nathan distinguishes modest above-chance prediction from certainty, describes experiments separating readiness potential, conscious decision, and movement, and concludes that the potential may reflect averaged noise or anticipation.
Indeterminism is not equivalent to randomness, and constrained variation can be integrated with deliberative selection and libertarian agency.

This answers the central luck objection to libertarianism by distinguishing mere absence of determination from randomness and offering constrained variation plus agent evaluation as a model of choice.
The hard-incompatibilist dilemma that every event is either determined or random and that neither alternative can constitute free agency.

Nathan rejects the proposed dichotomy as non-logical, explains probabilistic variation within constraints, and develops both brute choice and a neurophysical variation-and-selection model extending through the delivered boundary.
Weighted stochastic decision processes may still fail to provide the unrestricted authorship that incompatibilists associate with free will.
The move directly tests whether probabilistic alternatives improve on randomness enough to satisfy libertarian freedom and responsibility.
The earlier claim that constrained neural indeterminacy avoids the determined-or-random dilemma.
After Hawkins describes evolutionary variation and executive selection in the brain, Folley reconstructs how an incompatibilist might challenge probabilistically weighted choice.
If the self is identified with the brain's executive or valitional system, that self participates in setting the criteria governing indeterminate choice.
This supplies Hawkins's sourcehood answer by identifying the agent with the system that imposes constraints on indeterminate neural activity.
Folley's reconstruction of the incompatibilist demand for choice beyond a preset probability distribution.
Hawkins responds to the demand that the person, rather than probabilities, must choose by locating the person in the valitional system applying selection criteria.
Libertarian sourcehood need not require a detached soul because either agent causation or the conscious valitional brain can initiate the relevant action.
The move offers two accounts of agent sourcehood and argues that the neuroscientific model can meet the demand for a genuine initiating agent.
The suggestion that incompatibilists reject only a magical self hovering above physical processes.
Following discussion of whether traditional incompatibilism assumes a dualist will, Hawkins distinguishes agent causation from his preferred brain-based account of sourcehood.
A person's evaluative criteria are heavily constrained by genetics and upbringing, leaving much of the space of possible choices outside that person's control.
The objection targets ultimate sourcehood by shifting attention from indeterminate selection to the externally formed criteria that structure selection.
Hawkins's claim that the conscious valitional brain supplies the sourcehood incompatibilists request.
Folley grants the possible role of neural indeterminacy but argues that inherited and environmental factors still determine or restrict the criteria governing choice.
Libertarian freedom can operate within biological and social limits because agents contribute through repeated choices to their own long-term self-realization.
The response explains how meaningful agency and self-formation remain possible even when biology, society, and environment substantially constrain initial options.
Folley's objection that genetics and upbringing externally determine the criteria constraining later choices.
Hawkins concedes extensive external influence, then uses cumulative decisions and learning as examples of agents changing their brains and expanding future options.
An idealist but non-dualist metaphysics makes subjective deliberation fundamental and predicts a physical correlate of experienced choosing in the brain.
The move grounds his neuroscientific libertarian account in a broader metaphysics and defends taking first-person deliberative experience seriously.
The question whether Hawkins's libertarianism rests on broader philosophy or merely an intuition about deliberation.
Asked for the basis of his libertarian view, Hawkins explains that idealism treats physical brain activity as the manifestation of fundamentally mental reality.
Hawkins's limited libertarianism may deny the ultimate sourcehood and responsibility commonly sought when an agent's evaluative outlook is formed by a restrictive environment.
The example presses whether Hawkins can preserve robust moral responsibility when an agent never had meaningful access to alternative evaluative criteria.
Hawkins's claim that constrained agents still contribute to self-realization through indeterminate, criteria-guided choices.
Folley contrasts popular expectations of libertarian sourcehood with Hawkins's more modest model, using a socially isolated racist agent to expose the difference.
Compatibilism should reconstruct the practically important notions of freedom and will that survive determinism rather than claim that traditional libertarian freedom survives intact.
This is a direct constructive statement of the compatibilist position on the motion, identifying what agency can mean if determinism is assumed true.
After noting the long history of compatibilist ideas, Folley argues for preserving distinctions between chosen and unchosen conduct through rational and predictive models.
Indeterminate neuronal firing combined with system-level criterial constraints supplies uncaused neural events and top-down causation without requiring neurons to emerge from nothing.
The response addresses the physical mechanism at the heart of his libertarian view and distinguishes top-down agency from simple billiard-ball causation.
Folley's and hard incompatibilists' demand for a physically identifiable uncaused neural contribution to choice.
Invited to answer Folley's questions, Hawkins argues that firing can lack a sufficient determining cause while executive constraints operate downward at the system level.
Libertarian freedom requires alternatives that are genuinely live for the agent, so severe biological or social constraints can reduce freedom and moral responsibility by degree.
The move clarifies the scope of alternative possibilities in his libertarianism and states when constrained agents lack the responsibility normally tied to freedom.
Folley's racist-upbringing example and objection that restricted criteria undermine sourcehood and responsibility.
Hawkins accepts that biology and upbringing constrain options, but argues that freedom exists among live alternatives and responsibility diminishes when none are available.

A libertarian appeal to live options needs a principled account of when an alternative is genuinely available, especially because people continue to blame agents whose upbringing appears to exclude such alternatives.
The challenge directly tests whether alternative possibilities can explain responsibility judgments without an independent and workable criterion for identifying which possibilities were live.
Nathan Hawkins's claim that agents lacking any genuinely live alternative are not morally responsible.

After Hawkins treats biological and social constraints as compatible with freedom inside a remaining range of live options, Folley presses the epistemic boundary of that range and invokes responsibility judgments about Jojo.
Libertarian responsibility rests not merely on isolated present choices but on an agent's alternative-capable role in gradually shaping the character from which later settled conduct proceeds.
The move supplies both libertarian requirements named by the motion—doing otherwise and sourcehood—while explaining moral responsibility through cumulative self-formation under constraints.
Joe Folley's challenge that live-option restrictions resemble deterministic prediction and fail to match continuing blame of Jojo.

Hawkins answers the Jojo objection by arguing that respondents struggle to imagine a person wholly without resistance, then shifts from proximal choices to the accumulated decisions that form character.
Determinism can preserve will and responsibility through closed causal loops, proximal causation, and character models that predict an agent's conduct, without requiring genuine alternatives.
This is a direct compatibilist account of agency and responsibility under determinism, offering proximal sourcehood and causally effective character in place of libertarian alternatives.
Nathan Hawkins's contention that responsibility for character depends on alternative-capable choices made throughout a person's development.

Following Hawkins's cumulative self-formation account, Folley argues that upbringing can initiate a determined path while the resulting person still functions as a causal agent whose character explains later behavior.

Freedom and responsibility are plural, practice-shaped concepts whose useful content should be reconstructed from praise, blame, and reactive attitudes rather than forced into one metaphysically necessary-and-sufficient formula.
The move reframes the debate's governing standard: compatibilism need not reproduce one libertarian essence if multiple agency concepts successfully organize responsibility and social practice.
The libertarian framing that a single metaphysical condition of alternative possibility grounds and explains moral responsibility.

Folley notes that blame survives deterministic framing and that coercion can undermine freedom even with alternatives, then treats freedom, choice, and responsibility as related but nonidentical practical concepts.

If pragmatism takes deliberative phenomenology and practical causal reasoning seriously, it should regard agents as ultimate sources and their apparent ability to do otherwise as true rather than metaphysically irrelevant.
The argument seeks to derive both sourcehood and alternative possibilities from the compatibilist's own pragmatic starting point, directly supporting the libertarian side of the motion.
Joe Folley's pragmatic proposal to begin with the practical work of freedom and responsibility ascriptions rather than libertarian metaphysics.

Hawkins accepts the turn toward lived practices but argues that causal reasoning presents the deliberator as the originating cause, while responsibility practices treat unchosen alternatives as genuinely available.

The ineliminable first-person experience of deliberating as though one could do otherwise creates a serious unresolved challenge for a deterministic compatibilism that remains available from third-person perspectives.
This concession identifies a major internal pressure on compatibilism: deterministic theory may be sustainable for others while failing to govern the agent's own unavoidable deliberative standpoint.
Nathan Hawkins's argument that pragmatic attention to deliberation commits agents to subjective sourcehood and genuine alternatives.
Folley distinguishes a thicker pragmatist notion of truth from mere usefulness but accepts that he may be unable to understand his own deliberation without treating himself as able to do otherwise.

Because evolved conscious deliberation and inquiry are practically indispensable, pragmatism should validate their alternative-possibility structure, and interpersonal interpretation likewise resists denying agency to everyone except oneself.
The move strengthens the pragmatic case for alternatives and attacks the proposed first-person exception by arguing that ordinary interpretation also distinguishes genuine agency in other people.
Joe Folley's tentative position that first-person deliberation may require alternatives even though other agents can still be understood compatibilistically.

After Folley concedes a first-person difficulty, Hawkins argues first that evolution and inquiry vindicate deliberative alternatives and second that Folley's treatment of others already tracks agent-versus-excuse distinctions.

A proximal-source distinction between choices and nonchoices can survive proven determinism, while the conflict between objective study and first-person deliberation is a near-universal problem rather than a special failure of compatibilism.
The move offers a positive compatibilist basis for agency without alternatives and limits the force of the first-person objection by generalizing it across theories of human inquiry.
Nathan Hawkins's demand for a useful nonlibertarian source notion and his argument that deliberative agency extends to interpretations of other people.

Folley says deterministic truth would not erase the distinction between choices and nonchoices, then explains how inquiry becomes reflexively difficult once human deliberators are also treated as empirical objects.

Blurring the objective-subjective divide supports an idealist picture in which subjectivity belongs within the world itself, making nature's indeterminacy and selection more intelligible as mind-like rather than merely mechanical.

The proposal supplies a broader metaphysical setting in which libertarian subjectivity and natural indeterminacy can coexist, supporting sourcehood even though it is less direct than earlier arguments.
Joe Folley's claim that reconciling the human being as both inquirer and object of inquiry is a near-universal unresolved problem.
Hawkins treats pragmatism and idealism as responses to the collapse of a strict subject-object division, then suggests that patterns of randomness and selection indicate a more subject-like world.
